newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl optimistic about German economy, EMU prospects.
newsitem.headline: Kohl optimistic about German economy, EMU prospects.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl said Friday that German economic recovery was gathering pace and Bonn would fulfil the criteria to qualify for European economic and monetary union.
"For me it is clear. Germany will fulfil the criteria. The euro will come at the agreed time," Kohl said at his traditional semiannual news conference.
Kohl said the German economy was picking up speed and stuck by the official forecast of 2.5 percent growth this year. He said output could rise by as much as 3 percent in 1998.
"The main motor is exports. There are the first signs that the domestic economy is gaining momentum," he said.
Kohl played down the recent slide in the value of the mark to six-year lows below 1.80 to the dollar.

"When exports used to go badly because of a weak dollar, people complained," Kohl said. "Now things are going a bit the other way, which is not earth-shaking, it does not mean that we should start moaning again."

Kohl's remarks -- which followed repeated verbal support of the mark by both the Bonn government and the Bundesbank this week -- caused the dollar to tick up by around half a pfennig to trade at around 1.7980 at midday in Europe.

Separately, Finance Minister Theo Waigel said in Munich that the government would cut its deficit this year to 3 percent of GDP, despite pressures on the budget. He said the deficit would fall below the ceiling by "a sufficient margin" next year.

That view was disputed, however, by the independent IWH economic research institute. "Based on the current trends, I find 3.0 percent hard to imagine," IWH President Ruediger Pohl said in the east German town of Halle.
Pohl said, however, that a deficit of 3.4 percent of GDP this year should be no obstacle to Germany joining EMU at its planned start in 1999.
